title: Can School Choice Make Special Education Work? https://fordhaminstitute.org/national/commentary/can-school-choice-make-special-education-work
author: Daniel Buck
summary: Daniel Buck, a school choice supporter who distrusts claims that choice is a wonder drug, argues that choice may nonetheless be the best route to repairing American special education. He had earlier argued that eligibility had grown so loose that accommodations were harming both general and special education students, and had called for tighter federal guardrails under IDEA. Six months later he doubts that Washington can regulate its way out of a problem regulation created. He points to a new American Enterprise Institute report by Patrick Wolf and EdChoice researchers finding that students with disabilities make up 17.2 percent of choice-school enrollment versus 15 percent in traditional public schools, with high parental satisfaction. That undercuts the claim that choice leaves the hardest students behind. He acknowledges perverse incentives and unanswered questions about which disabilities are served, and concludes that the experiment is worth pushing further.
points: Buck's central claim is that school choice lets families assemble individualized services that a compliance-driven IEP process rarely delivers.
Students with disabilities are overrepresented in choice programs, which challenges the argument that public schools are left with the most challenging students.
Choice is politically feasible in a way that amending IDEA to add real accountability is not, and could attract bipartisan support if paired with funding.
Subsidizing higher voucher amounts for students with disabilities risks incentivizing more diagnoses, though existing programs require an IEP or a validated medical diagnosis.
He frames the conclusion as provisional, calling for more evidence rather than abandoning the federal entitlement outright.
quotes: Instead, let the sorting mechanism of school choice better allocate funds and services.
Conversely, in a choice-based system, parents can build a system that actually meets the unique needs of their child, securing a suite of individualized services and schooling options.
In choice schools, they represent 17.2 percent of enrolled students but only 15 percent of students within traditional public schools.
As it stands, this report undercuts one of the strongest arguments leveled against school choice programs: that they don’t serve all students.
Importantly, choice as a potential solution also has far greater political viability than head-on reform. Amending IDEA to introduce real accountability into the sector is a political nonstarter.
We still need to rethink special education, but regulation got us into this mess, and I don’t think Washington can regulate itself out.
I worry about the perverse incentives that a choice-based system would create, where students with special needs would receive larger vouchers or deposits in their ESA.
